title: Preparing diatom cell samples and bacterial consortia for SEM
author: Maillard, Stephant, et al.

steps.title: Prepare diatom culture
steps.instruction: Grow Phaeodactylum tricornutum to exponential phase at a target density of 9 × 10⁶ cells · mL⁻¹ starting from 1 × 10⁵ cells · mL⁻¹.

substeps.instruction: Take 50 µL of the stock culture, place on a Malassez cell and count to determine the current cell concentration.
Calculate the volume of culture needed to inoculate an Erlenmeyer flask containing Enhanced Artificial Sea Water medium so that the final concentration is 1 × 10⁵ cells · mL⁻¹.
Incubate the flask at 19 °C, shaking at 120 rpm, with a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle at 50 µE for 7 days to reach exponential growth.
Perform all handling in a laminar‑flow hood to maintain sterility.

steps.title: Make 10X PHEM buffer
steps.instruction: Prepare 200 mL of 10X PHEM buffer (pH 7.4) suitable for fixation.

substeps.instruction: In a beaker, dissolve EGTA, PIPES, HEPES and MgCl₂·6H₂O in distilled water; stir with a magnetic stirrer.
Adjust the solution volume to approximately 185 mL with distilled water.
In a separate beaker, dissolve 5 g NaOH in 15 mL distilled water; add this to the buffer mixture and check pH.
If pH is still >7.4, dissolve an additional 4 g NaOH in 15 mL distilled water and add dropwise until pH 7.4 is reached.
Bring the final volume to 200 mL with distilled water.

steps.title: Prepare washing buffer
steps.instruction: Make 200 mL of washing buffer (1.5X PHEM, 9 % w/v sucrose).

substeps.instruction: Mix 18 g sucrose into 30 mL of 1.5X PHEM buffer while stirring.
Add distilled water to bring the total volume to 200 mL.

steps.title: Prepare fixation buffer
steps.instruction: Prepare 10 mL of fixation buffer (for two samples) containing 9 % sucrose and 2.5 % glutaraldehyde in 1.5X PHEM.

substeps.instruction: Dissolve 0.9 g sucrose in 2 mL distilled water (9 % w/v).
Add 1.5 mL of the 10X PHEM buffer prepared above.
Add 2 mL of 25 % glutaraldehyde solution.
Adjust the final volume to 10 mL with distilled water.
Perform all steps in a laboratory fume hood because of glutaraldehyde.

steps.title: Fix diatom cells (Day 1)
steps.instruction: Fix the diatom culture with the prepared fixation buffer and incubate overnight at 4 °C.

substeps.instruction: Add 5 mL of the diatom culture to 5 mL of fixation buffer in a 15 mL Falcon tube.
Mix gently by inversion.
Incubate the tube overnight (≈17 h) at 4 °C.

steps.title: Centrifuge fixed cells (Day 2)
steps.instruction: Pellet the fixed cells and remove excess fixative while keeping the pellet slightly resuspended.

substeps.instruction: Centrifuge the tube at 2 200 g for 4 min at 4 °C.
Remove most of the supernatant, leaving ~200 µL to keep the pellet loosely resuspended.
Handle the tube in a fume hood because it still contains glutaraldehyde.

steps.title: Coat coverslips with poly‑L‑lysine
steps.instruction: Apply poly‑L‑lysine to clean coverslips, remove excess and dry.

substeps.instruction: Place clean coverslips in an empty Petri dish using forceps.
Pipette 100 µL of poly‑L‑lysine solution onto each coverslip and spread evenly.
Remove excess solution by pipetting it off.
Allow the coverslips to dry for >10 min at room temperature, keeping the Petri‑dish lid closed.
Record which side received the poly‑L‑lysine.

steps.title: Attach diatoms to coverslips
steps.instruction: Deposit the diatom pellet onto the poly‑L‑lysine‑coated coverslips and let cells settle on ice.

substeps.instruction: Place each coated coverslip in a separate well of a 24‑well plate (one coverslip per well).
Pipette 100 µL of the diatom pellet onto the coated side, spreading to cover the surface.
Keep the plate on ice for 1 h to allow cells to settle.
Handle any remaining fixation buffer in a fume hood.
Record which side contains both poly‑L‑lysine and diatoms.

steps.title: Wash coverslips
steps.instruction: Remove unattached cells and residual fixative by three gentle washes with washing buffer.

substeps.instruction: Add 1 mL washing buffer to each well, let stand 5 min at room temperature.
Remove the buffer with a pipette, pouring against the inner wall of the well (do not pour directly onto the coverslip).
Repeat the add‑incubate‑remove cycle two more times (total three washes).
Do not shake the plate to avoid dislodging attached diatoms.

steps.title: Dehydrate samples with ethanol
steps.instruction: Replace water in the samples with a graded ethanol series ending in absolute ethanol.

substeps.instruction: Prepare 50 mL each of 25 %, 50 %, 75 % ethanol and 50 mL of 100 % ethanol:
25 %: 12.5 mL absolute ethanol + 37.5 mL distilled water.
50 %: 25 mL absolute ethanol + 25 mL distilled water.
75 %: 37.5 mL absolute ethanol + 12.5 mL distilled water.
100 %: 50 mL absolute ethanol.
For each coverslip well, add 1 mL of 25 % ethanol, incubate 15 min at room temperature, then remove.
Repeat sequentially with 50 %, 75 % and 100 % ethanol, each for 15 min.
Perform a second 100 % ethanol bath and keep coverslips immersed in 100 % ethanol until critical‑point drying.
During all ethanol additions, pour the solution against the well wall and avoid shaking.

steps.title: Critical point dry samples
steps.instruction: Replace ethanol with liquid CO₂ in a critical‑point dryer and bring the samples to the supercritical state.

substeps.instruction: Place a biopsy cassette inside an empty Petri dish.
Fill the dish with absolute ethanol until the bottom of the cassette is covered.
Using forceps, transfer each coverslip from its well into the cassette.
Submerge the cassette in absolute ethanol and place it in the CPD chamber.
Close the chamber and start the CPD cycle:
i) Turn on the CPD unit and its cooling circuit.
ii) Open the CO₂ cylinder; allow the temperature to reach 10 °C.
iii) Fill the chamber with liquid CO₂, keeping the liquid level below the air bubble.
iv) Activate the stirrer, then drain the chamber down to the coverslip level.
v) Repeat the fill‑drain cycle 5–6 times (≈40 min) to fully replace ethanol with liquid CO₂.
vi) Stop the stirrer, close all valves, and turn on the heating circuit.
vii) Raise the temperature to 40 °C, which raises the pressure to 80–90 bar (≈10 min).
viii) Gradually reduce pressure with the Gas‑Out button and metering valve, never dropping below 80 bar (≈15 min) until supercritical CO₂ is achieved.
ix) Once stable, release pressure completely, open the chamber and retrieve the cassette.
Keep the coverslip side with diatoms clearly identified; if multiple samples are processed, cut the cassette with a scalpel to label each.
The coverslip must remain submerged in absolute ethanol from the end of dehydration until the CPD cycle begins.

steps.title: Mount and sputter coat coverslips
steps.instruction: Affix the dried coverslips to SEM stubs and apply a thin conductive metal layer.

substeps.instruction: Attach a carbon conductive tab to the top of a sample mount (SEM stub).
Place the coverslip onto the tab with the diatom‑covered side facing upward.
Apply a thin line of silver paint between the coverslip and the mount to ensure electrical contact.
Label each mount (e.g., with a number) and note the orientation of the diatom side.
Load the mounted coverslips into a sputter coater.
Run a coating cycle to deposit ~2 nm of platinum (or gold, Au‑Pd, or silver if Pt is unavailable) according to the coater’s instructions.

steps.title: Observe samples by SEM
steps.instruction: Image the diatom‑bacteria assemblies using a scanning electron microscope.

substeps.instruction: Insert the sample mount into the SEM chamber.
Set the acceleration voltage to approximately 5 kV.
Adjust beam intensity, working distance, and use a secondary‑electron detector for optimal surface contrast.
Set image acquisition speed to avoid beam‑induced damage.
Navigate to areas of interest, fine‑tune focus, astigmatism, contrast and brightness, and acquire images or measurements.
After imaging, store the mounts in a closed box at room temperature in the dark to prevent dust accumulation and degradation.

description: Diatoms, a crucial group of eukaryotic phytoplankton, are distributed across all latitudes in marine and freshwater ecosystems. They play a fundamental role in the biogeochemical cycling of elements such as carbon and silicon.1,2,3 They are responsible for around 45% of global primary production and yet represent only 1% of Earth’s photosynthetic biomass.4 In addition to their ecological importance, diatoms find widespread use in nanotechnology, aquaculture and in the pharmaceutical and industrial sectors.5,6 Diatoms do not live in isolation; they have coexisted with prokaryotes since early evolutionary stages. These interactions are critical for nutrient fluxes and the cycling of elements such as iron, nitrogen, vitamins, and phosphorus.3 Bacteria are crucial to microalgae as they supply essential components like vitamins, growth factors, iron and nitrogen among other benefits. In return, microalgae produce organic compounds through photosynthesis, which bacteria use as a carbon source. Both microalgae and bacteria enhance each other’s resilience to environmental conditions. Bacteria alter the microenvironment to make it more suitable for algal growth, while microalgae form biofilms that provide protection and facilitate nutrient exchange.7,8 Therefore, investigating these interactions at the electron microscopic scale will provide critical insights into their mechanisms, thereby advancing and complementing the knowledge acquired through other methods. Despite their significance in contributing to primary productivity at the base of the food chain, the nature of these interactions at the microscopic, specifically nanometer scale remains poorly understood. This knowledge gap is primarily due to the challenges in handling microscopic samples, particularly in liquid media.
